prompt.context: There are 8 balls that are identical in size and appearance. One of the balls is slightly lighter than the other seven.
prompt.question: How do you find the lighter ball using a balance scale, weighing only twice?

framework: Divide the 8 balls into groups to maximize information from each weighing
First weighing: split into two groups of 3, leaving 2 aside
Second weighing: narrow down within the lighter group of 3

questions.prompt: Walk through the step-by-step logic to identify the lighter ball in exactly two weighings.
questions.guidance: A strong answer systematically divides the balls to eliminate as many candidates as possible per weighing. Step 1: Take 6 of the 8 balls and weigh 3 against 3. Step 2a: If one side is lighter, the lighter ball is among those 3 — pick any 2 of the 3 and weigh them against each other. If one is lighter, that is the answer; if they balance, the third unweighed ball is the lighter one. Step 2b: If the first weighing balances (both sides equal), the lighter ball is one of the 2 set aside — weigh those 2 against each other; the lighter one is the answer. Either path resolves in exactly 2 weighings. The target solve time is within 10 seconds.

math.setup: 8 balls, 1 lighter; balance scale; maximum 2 weighings allowed
steps: Weighing 1: Place 3 balls on each side of the balance, set 2 aside
If one side tips up (lighter): the lighter ball is among those 3 — proceed to Weighing 2 with those 3
Weighing 2 (lighter group path): Weigh 1 ball vs 1 ball from the 3; if one side tips up it is the lighter ball; if they balance the third ball (not on the scale) is the lighter one
If Weighing 1 balances: the lighter ball is one of the 2 set aside — proceed to Weighing 2
Weighing 2 (set-aside path): Weigh the 2 set-aside balls against each other; the side that tips up is the lighter ball
math.answer: The lighter ball is identified in exactly 2 weighings in all possible scenarios

recommendation: Use a divide-and-conquer strategy: split into groups of 3-3-2 to guarantee identification in 2 weighings regardless of outcome
risks: Splitting into 4-4 for the first weighing leaves 4 candidates after one weighing, which cannot be resolved in one more weighing
Splitting into 2-2 wastes information capacity of the balance
